deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues a proof begun on the previous page.

Previous page, Lemma. Euler's four-square product identity, with A = a*alpha+b*beta+c*gamma+d*delta.

Previous page, Theorem. If N divides P^2+Q^2+R^2+S^2, with the squares not all divisible by N, then N is a sum of four squares.

Previous page, Step I. Reduce P, Q, R, S mod N to p, q, r, s with |p|,...,|s| < N/2. Then N n = p^2+q^2+r^2+s^2 with n < N.

Previous page, Step II. Write p = a + alpha n, q = b + beta n, r = c + gamma n, s = d + delta n.

THIS PAGE, continuation of the proof.

(II, end) Signed least residues are allowed, so |a|,|b|,|c|,|d| <= n/2. Hence a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 < n^2.

(III) Substituting gives
Nn = Σa^2 + 2n(aα+bβ+cγ+dδ) + n^2 Σα^2.
With A := aα+bβ+cγ+dδ (the first component in the lemma) this is
Nn = Σa^2 + 2nA + n^2 Σα^2.
The left side and the last two terms are divisible by n, so n | Σa^2. Put Σa^2 = n n'. Dividing by n:
N = n' + 2A + n Σα^2.

(IV) Multiply by n' and replace n n' by Σa^2:
N n' = n'^2 + 2n'A + (Σa^2)(Σα^2).
By the four-square identity (Σa^2)(Σα^2) = A^2+B^2+C^2+D^2, where for instance B = aβ−bα+cδ−dγ, etc. (explicit B, C, D are mine). Hence
N n' = (n'+A)^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2.

(V) Since n n' = Σa^2 < n^2, we get n' < n. Iterating gives a decreasing sequence n > n' > n'' > ... of multipliers m with N m a sum of four squares. The sequence must reach 1, so N itself is a sum of four squares.

Corollary 1. Euler claims the argument works for composite N as well: any divisor of a sum of four squares is a sum of four squares.

Corollary 2. Hence Fermat's four-square theorem would be complete if one showed that every N divides some sum of four squares. By multiplicativity it suffices to do this for primes N.

NEW THEOREM. For a prime N there exist four squares, each < N^2/4, whose sum is divisible by N. The bound comes from taking residues in (−N/2, N/2).

Proof (begun here).
(I) Every integer lies in one of the classes λN + k, k = 0, ..., N−1. Set aside k = 0. Since x^2 ≡ (N−x)^2, the classes 1 and N−1 contribute squares to the same class λN+1. Likewise 2 and N−2 go to λN+4, and 3 and N−3 to λN+9, and so on. So exactly (N−1)/2 nonzero classes contain squares, and the other (N−1)/2 contain none.
(II) Name the residue classes a, b, c, d, ... (they include 1, 4, 9, 16, ... while these are < N; larger squares are reduced mod N). Name the non-residue classes α, β, γ, δ, ...; there are also (N−1)/2 of them.

Next page. The multiplicative rules R·R = R, R·N = N, N·N = R are used. Then the argument shows −1 is a non-residue under the hypothesis that no sum of two or three squares is divisible by N. From this, f residue ⇒ f+1 residue, so every class would be a residue: a contradiction. This is Euler's proof that some x^2+y^2+z^2 (indeed x^2+y^2+1) is ≡ 0 mod N.
errors: Step II/V: 'infra 1/2 n' with strict inequality is not always attainable. For even n the least absolute residue can be ±n/2, so only Σa^2 <= n^2. Equality (all residues ±n/2) gives n' = n and the descent stalls. Euler does not treat this case. It can be excluded for prime N: then n divides each of p,q,r,s minus n/2, which forces n | N, impossible for 1 < n < N.

Unhandled case n' = 0. If Σa^2 = 0 then n divides p, q, r, s, so n^2 | Nn and n | N. For prime N with 1 < n < N this is impossible. For composite N (Corollary 1) the descent then breaks down, so the proof as written does not cover composite N without extra argument (e.g. a gcd condition or factoring). Corollary 1 is nonetheless true, as a consequence of Lagrange's theorem.

The hypothesis 'not each divisible by N' (previous page) is not the right condition. What is needed is essentially that the reduced residues p, q, r, s are not all 0, which suffices to give n >= 1. For composite N one also needs control of common factors.

Step I of the new theorem: Euler asserts there are exactly (N−1)/2 square-containing classes without proving that 1^2, 2^2, ..., ((N−1)/2)^2 are pairwise incongruent. This requires N prime: N | (x−y)(x+y). He also tacitly assumes N is odd.
'per lemma praemissum abit in hanc': this step is merely the definition A = aα+bβ+cγ+dδ, not an application of the lemma. Harmless.
Next page: 'facile demonstrari potest' for the product rules (especially non-residue × non-residue = residue) is asserted without proof. That rule needs a counting argument.

results.what: Descent: if prime N divides a sum of four squares (not all ≡ 0 mod N), then N is a sum of four squares. Uses the four-square identity and N n' = (n'+A)^2+B^2+C^2+D^2 with n' < n.
results.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange descent step in the proof of Lagrange's four-square theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (E242, written ~1751, publ. 1760) with Lagrange (1770) completing the theorem; the descent in this form is Euler's

results.what: Corollary 2: Fermat's four-square theorem reduces to showing that every (prime) N divides some sum of four squares.
results.modern_name: Reduction of the four-square theorem to the local (mod p) solvability of x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2 ≡ 0

results.what: For prime N, exactly (N−1)/2 nonzero residue classes contain squares. This begins a proof, completed on the next page, that some sum of three (indeed x^2+y^2+1) squares is divisible by N.
results.modern_name: Count of quadratic residues; solvability of x^2+y^2+1 ≡ 0 (mod p)

results.what: Corollary 1: any divisor of a sum of four squares is a sum of four squares.
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange 1770 (Euler's proof here is incomplete for composite N)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a version of Euler's well-known four-square work. It contains the descent via his four-square identity and the quadratic-residue argument for x^2+y^2+1 ≡ 0 mod p, both of which appear in his published papers (E242 and related). It was printed in the Opera Postuma (1862) among the 'Fragmenta ex adversariis'. Nothing here goes beyond what historians already attribute to him; the only points of interest are minor variants of presentation and the gaps for even n and composite N.
